lessons.title: das Brot — "bread"
lessons.gloss: bread — and the third article, das, which completes the set you were given in chapter one

segments.text: Der Vater. Die Mutter. You were given a third article in the first chapter and have had no noun for it. Here it is.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: das Brot

segments.text: das Brot — "bread."
A das-word. That completes the set on real nouns: der Vater, die Mutter, das Brot — one of each, and now you have met all three doing their job rather than sitting in a list.
long-o — a long o, the vowel of English boat, held steady.
r-uvular — the r is made far back in the throat.
d-t-final — and the final t is crisp.
broht. One syllable, and capitalised on the page like every German noun, whether it names a person or a loaf.

segments.text: "das Brot."

Say "bread." (Das Brot.) Which article? (Das — the neuter.) Say all three with a noun each. (Der Vater, die Mutter, das Brot.) Why the capital B? (German capitalises every noun.) Next: where the word comes from, and where it does not.

lessons.title: Brot and bread
lessons.gloss: the word Rome did not supply — where French says pain, German kept its own

segments.text: A word can be interesting for what happened to it. This one is interesting for what did not.
Brot comes from Germanic braudam, and English bread comes from the same word. No Latin anywhere in it.
Now the other side of the line. Latin pānis went into every Romance language and stayed there:

utterances: language: German. the word: Brot. from: Germanic braudam.
language: French. the word: pain. from: Latin pānis.
language: Italian. the word: pane. from: Latin pānis.

segments.text: Rome sold German a calendar and a clock. It did not sell German bread.

The pattern is the one you have been given four times now and it holds again here: a thing people handle every single day already has a word, and an incoming language does not get to replace it. Months were an administrative object and arrived with their labels. A loaf on a table was not waiting for a name.
That is why Brot sits with Vater and Mutter rather than with Januar.

segments.text: "Brot, bread."
What is the English twin of Brot? (Bread.) What does French say? (Pain, from Latin pānis.) Did German borrow that? (No.) Why not? (A daily thing already had a word.) Next: the second of the three.

lessons.title: das Wasser — "water"
lessons.gloss: water — a second das-word, and the w that is said as a v

segments.text: Bread, and then something to drink beside it. Its first letter you have met twice already.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: das Wasser

segments.text: das Wasser — "water."
Another das-word, so it takes the same article as Brot. Two neuters in a row is a useful accident: it lets you say das Brot und das Wasser without having to decide anything.
w-as-v — German w is an English v. Wasser opens VAH-.
vowel-a-german — a clean open a.
r-final — and the soft closing r.
VAH-ser. You have had that w on Winter, and inside the shv- of Schwester; this is the third time and the first where it sits on its own at the front of a word.

segments.instruction: "das Wasser" — VAH-ser
the letter and the sound — "W on the page, v in the mouth"

segments.instruction: the two together — "das Brot und das Wasser"

segments.text: "das Wasser."
Say "water." (Das Wasser.) Which article? (Das, like Brot.) How is the W said? (As a v.) Where did you meet that before? (On Winter, and inside Schwester.) Next: its English twin.

lessons.title: Wasser and water
lessons.gloss: one Germanic root, and the German shift you can hear in the middle of it

segments.text: Say Wasser and then water. The difference is one consonant, and you have met it before.
Both come from Germanic watar. English kept the t. German turned it into ss.

That is German's own later shift — the second of the two you met on Mutter, where English stopped at mother and German kept going. It ran through the vocabulary the same way, so once you have it you can predict it:
Two chapters, four inherited words, and the same two shifts explaining every difference between the German and the English.

That is the payoff of a sound law: you stop memorising pairs. Wasser is not a word to be learned beside water — it is water, with one predictable change applied, and the change is one you can now run yourself.
And like Brot, nothing here was bought. Water is as everyday as a word gets.

what changed — "t became ss"

segments.text: "Wasser, water."

What is the English twin? (Water.) What did German do to the t? (Made it ss.) Which other word did the same shift? (Mutter.) Inherited or borrowed? (Inherited.) Next: the one on this table that was borrowed.

lessons.title: der Wein — "wine"
lessons.gloss: wine — a der-word, and the one thing on this table Rome supplied

segments.text: Two das-words so far. The third drink takes a different article, and that is the smaller of the two things different about it.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: der Wein

segments.text: der Wein — "wine."
A der-word, where Brot and Wasser are both das. So the three now run one of each: das Brot, das Wasser, der Wein.
w-as-v — the W is a v again, as in Wasser.
diphthong-ei — and ei is the vowel of English eye, which you were given on eins.
Put the two together and Wein comes out sounding like English vine. Hold on to that, because the next lesson is about why.

segments.instruction: "der Wein" — like English "vine"
the two vowels you know — "ei is eye, as in eins"

segments.text: "der Wein."
Say "wine." (Der Wein.) Which article? (Der — not das, like the other two.) What does ei sound like? (English eye.) So what English word does it sound like? (Vine.) Next: why it does.

lessons.title: Wein and vinum
lessons.gloss: not three cousins but one loan — the vine came north and its name came with it

segments.text: Wasser and water differ by a consonant. Wein and wine differ by nothing you can hear. That difference is the lesson.
Wein is not an inherited Germanic word. It was borrowed from Latin vīnum in Roman times, when the legions brought the grapevine north of the Alps.
Here is how you can tell without being told. Inherited words drift apart, because a sound law runs through them:

utterances: pair: Wasser / water. how far apart: a whole consonant — ss against t.
pair: Mutter / mother. how far apart: two shifts of distance.
pair: Wein / wine / vīnum. how far apart: no distance at all.

segments.text: Three words that match this closely are not three cousins who happen to look alike. They are one word, borrowed, arriving too late for the law to touch it.

The vine did not grow north of the Alps until Rome carried it there. A people who have never had a thing have no word for it, and when the thing arrives the word arrives with it — which is the same reason Uhr is Latin and the twelve months are Latin.
So one table holds both halves of the rule. Brot and Wasser were always here and are German's own. Wein came on a cart, and its name was in the same load.

segments.text: "Wein, wine, vinum — one loan."
Is Wein inherited? (No — borrowed from Latin vīnum.) How can you tell? (It is too close — a law would have moved it.) What arrived with the word? (The grapevine.) And Wasser? (Always here.)

lessons.title: Practice — one table, two histories
lessons.gloss: chapter payoff — three words on one table, two of them German's own and one on loan

segments.text: No new words. Three things you could put on a table, and one of them is a different kind of word from the other two.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: three nouns, three articles

segments.text: Two neuters and a masculine, every one of them capitalised. There is no rule behind which is which — the article comes with the noun and is learned with it, which is why every word in this book arrives wearing one.
Now the histories, which do have a rule behind them:
Brot — Germanic braudam, English bread. French took Latin pānis and German did not.
Wasser — Germanic watar, English water, with German's own later shift turning the t into ss.
Wein — Latin vīnum, borrowed whole, matching English wine and the Latin too closely to be anything else.

Two were always here; one came north on a cart with the plant it names. You can read that off the words themselves without knowing any history: the inherited pair have drifted from their English twins, and the borrowed one has not.
